title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in St. Louis, MO: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for St. Louis aerospace, refinery, pipeline and bridge welders: Parts A, B and C, online or at your Missouri or Illinois site.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in St. Louis, Missouri: Six Days of Preparation for a Two-State Welding Market
html:
The St. Louis region straddles two states and two big rivers, and its welding work is just as split: military aircraft on the Missouri side, a large refinery and crude pipelines on the Illinois side, steel bridges across the Mississippi, and hundreds of fabricators, barge yards and contract shops in between. A welder or QC technician who wants to become an AWS Certified Welding Inspector here can end up working to four or five different codes in a career. Atlantis NDT runs a six-day (6-day) exam-preparation course for the AWS CWI examination, aimed at people in that position. The American Welding Society sets the eligibility rules, administers the exam and awards the CWI; Atlantis helps you prepare and has no role in scoring. Request a St. Louis quote to get started.

The six-day course, briefly

The course follows the three parts of the AWS exam. Days one and two cover Fundamentals: processes, terms, joint design, welding symbols, metallurgy, testing, discontinuities, safety and inspector duties. Day three rehearses the Part B practical. Day four is code application in the book you pick for Part C. Day five is timed mock papers, and day six is targeted review and exam-day logistics. The full outline sits on the national AWS CWI exam prep page.

How you take it depends on who is paying. Someone preparing on their own studies online at their own pace, using the plan, reading, original practice items and an instructor reachable by message for questions. A company with a handful of candidates can book the six days at its own site in Missouri or Illinois. Atlantis keeps no training room in St. Louis and posts no class calendar. AWS has neither endorsed nor approved the course, and the practice items are Atlantis's own writing, never questions lifted from an AWS paper.

Where St. Louis welding inspectors actually work

It helps to see the region as a set of separate markets, because each one leans on a different code and a different kind of inspection.

Military aircraft and the aerospace supply chain

Boeing's defense business builds fighters, trainers and unmanned aircraft at its St. Louis site, and a wide network of machine shops, sheet-metal houses and tube benders around the region supplies parts to aerospace customers. Aerospace welding is mostly thin-section gas tungsten arc work on steels, nickel alloys, titanium and aluminum, where a small porosity cluster or a crater crack can reject a part. The governing documents are usually the customer's own specification, often built on AWS D17.1, the fusion welding specification for aerospace applications, which is one of the books AWS lets you choose for Part C. A shop inspector in this world spends less time with a fillet gauge and more time with a magnifier, a drawing and a traveler.

The refinery and the crude pipeline corridor

Across the river in Roxana, Illinois, the Wood River Refinery operated by Phillips 66 is one of the largest industrial sites in the region, and turnaround seasons bring in contract pipefitters and welders by the hundreds. Process piping repair and replacement is welded and inspected to ASME B31.3, with procedures and welders qualified under ASME Section IX. Farther east, the Patoka area in southern Illinois is a major junction for crude oil pipelines, and new line construction or station work is welded to API 1104. Either job wants inspectors who can verify a welder's qualification range, watch preheat and confirm visual acceptance before radiography or ultrasonic examination by a licensed contractor.

Bridges over the Mississippi and Missouri

The region depends on long-span river crossings, from the historic Eads Bridge to the cable-stayed Stan Musial Veterans Memorial Bridge that carries Interstate 70. Steel girders and repairs on structures like these are fabricated and welded to AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code, with fracture-critical members held to stricter rules. The Missouri and Illinois departments of transportation and their consultants inspect that work, and fabricators supplying it staff their quality control with certified welding inspectors.

River equipment, food plants and contract manufacturing

St. Louis is one of the country's busiest inland port regions, and barge and towboat building and repair along the river is heavy plate welding in all positions. The city's breweries, food processors and pharmaceutical plants run stainless sanitary piping, often welded to AWS D18.1, which is not a Part C option, so candidates from those plants usually take D1.1 or the ASME book. Add the structural steel fabricators serving warehouses, data centers and hospital expansions, and the result is a market where a CWI rarely runs out of work.

Building inspection on larger projects

Building departments on both sides of the river enforce the special inspection chapter of the International Building Code on bigger structural projects. Structural steel welding is one of the listed special inspections, so an independent agency hired by the owner watches welding on site and reviews shop welding records, separate from the fabricator's own quality control. The agencies doing that work around St. Louis tend to send CWIs, because the role means checking welder qualifications against the job, verifying joint preparation before the root pass, and writing up nonconforming welds in a way a structural engineer will accept. If you like variety, special inspection moves you from a hospital frame one month to a stadium canopy or a distribution center the next.

Matching the Part C code to your St. Louis job

AWS lets each candidate choose the code for the open-book part. The options it lists include AWS D1.1 for structural steel, API 1104 for pipelines, AWS D1.2 for aluminum structures, AWS D1.5 for bridges, AWS D15.1 for railcars and locomotives, AWS D17.1 for aerospace, and an ASME option combining Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3. The edition on the exam is the one AWS names, which can be older than the newest printing, so check before you buy a book.

  • Aerospace supply chain: D17.1, if your employer's specifications are built on it.
  • Refinery and petrochemical maintenance: the ASME Section IX with B31.3 option.
  • Pipeline construction and stations: API 1104. See the API 1104 overview and API 1104 acceptance criteria.
  • Bridge and highway steel: D1.5. See AWS D1.5.
  • General structural, barges and contract fabrication: D1.1.

If you are unsure, pick the code you use at work. The certificate shows which book you were examined on, and an employer will read that as evidence of what you know best.

The AWS St. Louis Section

St. Louis has its own AWS section within District 14. Its calendar includes an annual Weld Show each spring that brings together educators, students, working welders, suppliers and industry people for demonstrations and networking, and a summer golf outing on the Illinois side. The section also has a student chapter at Lewis & Clark Community College. For a CWI candidate the value is practical. Section events are where you meet the inspectors and supervisors who can vouch for your welding-related experience, where you hear which fabricators and contractors are short of inspection staff, and where you can ask a working CWI how the Part B practical felt. Check the section's website through aws.org for current dates.

Welding schools that feed inspection careers here

Most people who reach the CWI exam in St. Louis started behind a hood. Three local programs come up often:

  • Ranken Technical College runs a Fabrication and Welding Technology program in the city.
  • St. Louis Community College offers Welding Technology certificates at different levels.
  • Lewis & Clark Community College in Godfrey, Illinois, hosts the AWS student chapter mentioned above and runs welding instruction on the Illinois side.

Formal schooling matters for the CWI because AWS trades education against years of welding-related experience. A high school diploma means five years of qualifying work; recognized trade or vocational courses, an associate degree or welding-related engineering study each reduce that, down to one year with a bachelor's in welding engineering or welding technology. Keep transcripts and certificates handy, because AWS decides how your schooling is classed. Ironworker, boilermaker and pipefitter apprenticeships in the region also build the kind of documented experience the application asks for.

Getting to the exam from St. Louis

The exam comes in two formats. Parts A and C are computer-based and booked at a Prometric center using the eligibility code on your AWS confirmation letter; AWS says there are more than one hundred such centers across the United States, so look up the closest one on Prometric's site. Part B, the practical, is delivered by AWS at its seminar and exam locations on fixed dates, and US applications for Part B close about six weeks ahead. Look at the AWS seminar and examination schedule early and plan any travel around it.

The numbers to keep in mind: 150 questions on Part A, 46 questions alongside the hands-on Part B tasks, roughly 50 to 65 open-book questions on Part C, and a minimum of 72% on each. Prometric gives up to two hours of exam time per computer-based part. AWS posts current exam and seminar fees on aws.org; the CWI cost planner helps you budget the whole process, including travel for Part B.

A preparation timeline that works around St. Louis jobs

Turnarounds at the refinery, overtime on aircraft programs and seasonal river work all eat into study time. A plan that tends to hold up looks like this:

  1. Twelve to sixteen weeks out: confirm you meet the experience rule, book the AWS vision examination on the current form, choose your Part C book and apply.
  2. Ten weeks out: work through the two Fundamentals days online, drilling welding symbols until you can read them without looking up the chart.
  3. Eight weeks out: start living in your code book. Tab it the way the exam rules allow and practice finding tables for preheat, acceptance and qualification ranges.
  4. Six weeks out: rehearse Part B skills with real gauges on scrap welds from work. Measure, record, then decide.
  5. Three weeks out: sit the timed mock papers and send the instructor whatever you got wrong.
  6. Last week: review weak areas only, confirm Prometric and Part B logistics, and stop learning new material.

On-site groups compress the same content into six consecutive days at the employer's facility, then use the remaining weeks before the exam for self-study.

Bringing the six days to a Missouri or Illinois facility

For fabricators, contractors and manufacturers with several candidates, on-site delivery is usually the better fit. The practical day can use the shop's own gauges and real joints from production, and the code day can run in whatever book the company builds to, whether that is D1.1 for structural work, D1.5 for bridge girders or the ASME option for piping. Mixed groups are common in St. Louis: a structural shop may have one person on API 1104 because of field pipeline work. The course handles that by splitting the code day. Remember that AWS deals with each candidate as an individual; the company cannot file applications or vision records for them.

What comes after the CWI in St. Louis

Under the AWS rules the CWI runs for nine years in total, with renewal paperwork at the three-year and six-year points and a recertification step at the end. Inspectors here tend to build on it in a few ways. Shop inspectors in aerospace and fabrication often add nondestructive testing methods, because visual acceptance is only the first gate. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, an employer certifies its NDT technicians after method training and documented experience; Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A-based training (see NDT training for St. Louis and VT Level 1 training). Refinery inspectors often aim at API in-service inspection certifications, which API runs on its own terms and which Atlantis does not train for. Others move into supplier quality or step up to Senior CWI. For local inspection context, see visual testing in St. Louis and penetrant testing in St. Louis.

If you are still deciding between welding inspection and NDT, read welding inspector vs NDT technician and the CWI requirements and career guide.

Neighboring CWI prep pages and your quote

Candidates in the middle of the country also look at CWI exam prep for Kansas City, Indianapolis and Tulsa.

To price the course, list the number of candidates, sketch each one's schooling and welding history, note which Part C code each expects to take, and, for delivery at your site, give the address and the inspection tools you already own. Send that through the St. Louis quote request and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can I take CWI exam prep in a St. Louis classroom?
faq.a: Atlantis has no classroom in St. Louis. People preparing alone work the six-day material online with an instructor to message; companies can book the six days at their own Missouri or Illinois site. Course outline.
No. AWS runs the examination and grants the CWI to candidates who meet its eligibility rules and pass. Atlantis prepares people for the exam and has no AWS approval or endorsement.

faq.q: Which Part C code suits aerospace work in St. Louis?
faq.a: If your employer's welding specifications are built on AWS D17.1, choose D17.1, which AWS lists as a Part C option. Aerospace shops with structural or tooling work sometimes choose D1.1 instead.

faq.q: I work refinery turnarounds at Wood River. Which code should I pick?
faq.a: Most refinery maintenance inspectors pick the ASME book, which pairs Section IX with the power and process piping codes, because process piping repair is qualified and inspected to those books. Pipeline people choose API 1104; see API 1104.

faq.q: Where is the nearest CWI exam to St. Louis?
faq.a: Parts A and C are taken at a Prometric center, and AWS says more than one hundred operate in the US. Part B is run by AWS at its seminar and exam sites on set dates, so check the AWS schedule and allow for travel.

faq.q: How many years of experience do I need?
faq.a: It depends on schooling. With a high school diploma AWS asks for five years of welding-related work; trade courses, an associate degree or welding engineering study reduce that. See the CWI requirements guide.

faq.q: Can our fabrication shop host the six days?
faq.a: Yes. On-site delivery practises on joints from your production with your gauges, and the code day runs in your book. Ask for a quote.

faq.q: Is the AWS St. Louis Section worth joining before the exam?
faq.a: Yes for most candidates. Section events such as the spring Weld Show put you in front of working inspectors who can confirm your experience and tell you which employers need CWIs.

faq.q: Does the course include real AWS questions?
faq.a: No. Atlantis writes its own practice items to the published AWS subject areas and never sees the actual exam. For method practice, try the free NDT practice tests.

faq.q: Should I learn NDT after becoming a CWI?
faq.a: In aerospace and fabrication shops, adding penetrant, magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing widens what you can inspect. Your employer certifies you under SNT-TC-1A after training and experience. See NDT training for St. Louis.
